page: Microsoft Azure L8s_v4 is a storage-optimized virtual machine instance running on the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is powered by an x86_64 Intel Xeon 8573C processor featuring 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped across 4 physical cores with multithreading enabled, reaching clock speeds up to 4.2 GHz. The CPU architecture incorporates a 260 MB L3 cache alongside advanced hardware extensions, including AVX-512 and AMX instructions for matrix acceleration. The platform is configured with 64.0 GB of system memory, yielding an 8.0 GB per-core allocation. Storage is directly integrated with a 1920 GB local NVMe SSD, while discrete GPU acceleration is absent.

Performance evaluation shows solid compute and throughput capabilities across standard benchmarks. The Intel processor delivers strong single-core results, scoring 2168.0 on Geekbench and reaching 31.37 GB/sec in single-threaded gzip compression. Multithreaded execution aligns with midrange expectations for an 8-vCPU footprint, producing a multi-core Geekbench score of 8333.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 14267.95. Memory bandwidth reaches 65.68 GB/sec read and 45.55 GB/sec write on large blocks. Key-value performance registers 11.48 million operations per second during Redis SET benchmarks, complemented by 14.97 GB/sec in static web serving throughput. Because the server lacks dedicated accelerator hardware, text generation on larger language models remains constrained, with medium 7B models achieving 8.36 tokens per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the bundled 1.92 TB local NVMe storage provides high density and local throughput without incurring separate network block storage provisioning overheads. The balanced 8:1 RAM-to-vCPU ratio and high single-core frequency make it efficient for high-throughput I/O pipelines. The primary operational tradeoff involves the ephemeral nature of local NVMe storage, requiring data replication for stateful applications, alongside limited compute capacity for deep learning inference. The hardware profile fits transactional relational databases, NoSQL engines, in-memory data grids, search indexing, and real-time log analytics.
